props.title: Femme Fatale

sections.content: Brian De Palma's Femme Fatale masterfully updates film noir conventions for the digital age. Like his earlier Body Double (1984) and Dressed to Kill (1980), De Palma crafts an intricate puzzle box of identity and deception. The opening heist at Cannes Film Festival - a 20-minute sequence with minimal dialogue - showcases his virtuoso camera movement and split-screen techniques that echo Sisters (1972). Rebecca Romijn plays a duplicitous jewel thief with the same dangerous allure Barbara Stanwyck brought to Double Indemnity (1944).

sections.content: De Palma's signature split-screens and voyeuristic camera create a hypnotic dreamscape in Femme Fatale. The film's complex narrative structure, with its parallel realities and time loops, pushes noir into postmodern territory like Mulholland Drive (2001). The director's obsession with Alfred Hitchcock surfaces in direct homages to Vertigo (1958), particularly in scenes of doubling and identity theft. Antonio Banderas brings a wounded intensity as the photographer drawn into Laure's web of deceit.

The film's stunning opening sequence during a screening of East-West (1999) establishes the meta-cinematic playfulness that defines De Palma's style. Like Blow Out (1981) and Body Double (1984), Femme Fatale explores the relationship between watching and being watched, reality and illusion. The director's trademark split-screen techniques reach their apex here, creating parallel narratives that eventually collapse into each other. SUBHEAD: De Palma's Visual Innovation

sections.content: The director's technical mastery reaches new heights in Femme Fatale. His floating camera movements recall the dream logic of Raising Cain (1992), while the complex heist sequence rivals Mission: Impossible (1996) for sustained tension. De Palma's split-screen technique evolves beyond simple parallel action into a tool for exploring alternate realities, predating similar experiments in Inception (2010).
